unknown: Offer a substitute when, by your own judgement, it is close enough that the customer could use it.
The apology discount on a substitute is the smallest discount: about 1% when your authority runs 1 to 5%. It is a token of goodwill.

If there is no way to meet it, apologize, say it cannot be done as asked and explain what can: if they wait, it ships on the restock date, with about 2% off for the wait (when your authority runs 1 to 5%).
Apologize for any delay even if there was no earlier acknowledgement, and say it will be done as quickly as possible.
As the delay gets longer, raise the discount a little within your authority, and give a clear reason for the delay.
Apologize on a first-time request too; a customer is a customer.
If the customer insists strongly, do not offer partial shipment or waiting.
If the customer later relents, give the smallest discount, about 1%, as a token of goodwill.
Ask once: is it this item, is it one of these, and if not, please describe it a little more. Check what they send back against the catalog, then say it is not available or that this is the item.
If the confirmed code is still not in the catalog, it may not be ours: ask for whatever else they know and say the shop will look into it.
When several similar items come up, ask the customer whether it is one of these; do not pick one. The aim is to find the item they want.
This applies to every request: the ship date matters almost as much as the item. Matching the date the customer has in mind with the date the shop can do comes first.
If the customer never gives a date, quote the earliest date the shop can ship and say in the reply that it is the earliest date the shop can offer.
Telling the customer the earliest ship date is standard; shipping as early as possible also saves storage cost.
A buffer is good: when the customer's latest date is after the earliest date the shop can ship, set the date 1 to 2 days before their latest date.
The exact size of the buffer is a judgement call: 1 or 2 days, normally business days.
Count business days (in Korea people say 1 to 2 business days); it may differ by country.
A quote that expires today still counts: a quote holds through its date, so honor it.
Still check stock and the ship date again: stock can change, and the quote only holds the price.
A change in cost or discount authority does not override it: an earlier quote within its valid date comes first, and keeping that price keeps the customer's trust.
Always state clearly that the quote expired, to keep trust and avoid misunderstanding.
Do not offer a discount first. Only after the customer complains and asks for a cut, give the smallest discount (1%), because selling beats not selling.
Always recalculate from the current cost, then discount if needed. Never match the old price.
Always ask the owner about any discount beyond your authority.
Bring a request to the owner when the customer pushes hard and buys a lot, or is an important customer.

Do not discount without an explicit request. On a re-quote, when the customer explicitly asks for a lower price, give the smallest discount; a regular customer may get a little more. If it goes beyond your authority, judge again and pass it to the owner if the customer seems important.
If stock is short, say so and first ask whether the earliest possible date works; the rest follows from that.
Order of work: confirm the item first, then check stock, then discount if a discount is called for.
Never skip the stock check on a re-quote: stock differs at every moment, and other clerks may be selling the same stock.
